title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—a single shared LLM candidate (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a concise post‑hoc sensitivity analysis tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Automating translation of operator intent to device configuration can speed NetOps but introduces operational risk when generated outputs are incomplete, misordered, or otherwise unsafe. Prior surveys and system demonstrations report promise but also recurring failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—leading practitioners to recommend guarded architectures that pair probabilistic generation (LLMs) with deterministic validators or simulators as floor‑safety nets. Despite these proposals, there are few preregistered, paired A/B experiments measuring whether bounded generate→verify→repair pipelines concretely reduce first‑pass misconfiguration. To fill that experimental gap, we implemented a narrowly scoped preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline: a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot), a frozen deterministic validator performing rule and dependency checks, and at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. Our central question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce the first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Principal contributions are (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic seeds and full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) artifact‑grounded confirmatory statistics showing a near‑ceiling baseline and a single corrected discordance; (3) a compact post‑hoc sensitivity analysis derived from the archived contingency counts; (4) practical recommendations for designing future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Recent NetOps work demonstrates LLMs can synthesize configuration templates and perform intent translation in controlled settings, while surveys and cross‑domain studies show verifier‑assisted loops and deterministic safety nets reduce factual errors in domain tasks. Architectural proposals for agentic NetOps commonly endorse generate→verify→repair patterns and deterministic validators as floor guards. However, the published literature contains few preregistered experiments that (a) use deterministic paired sampling semantics, (b) freeze validator logic prior to execution, and (c) bound automated repair iterations under a confirmatory analysis plan. Our experiment is positioned at the intersection of these recommendations and addresses the practical question of whether a minimal guarded pipeline yields measurable first‑pass improvements under preregistered paired inference.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the study as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 and froze the experimental plan before execution. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 for power calculations (this numeric assumption is reported here per reviewer guidance and is archived in the preregistration record). For planning the preregistration noted that with N=300 pairs the design had >80% power to detect absolute paired differences ≥0.20 at α=0.05 under conservative discordant assumptions.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from a frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics) was used for both arms: baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The preregistered decision to reuse the shared candidate per pair increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference; this choice and its inferential consequences were prespecified. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Model, validator, and scoring: Declared model = gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule and dependency checks, canonicalizes configurations to normalized ASTs, and emits binary pass/fail scoring with violation codes used to decide repair actions. Scoring semantics are full intent‑constraint validation: success requires the validator to confirm required command sequences and dependency constraints. Provider/model failures were handled per the preregistered missingness plan (one retry allowed; primary analysis 'complete_pair_primary' drops pairs only if both calls fail).

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The prespecified primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. We report the absolute risk difference and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, fixed seed) as preregistered. Secondary analyses included repair success rate with exact binomial intervals and sensitivity checks for missingness and contamination. All analytical code and per‑task artifacts were archived; the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle enumerate the archived items and their integrity metadata.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifact completeness: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301. Under the preregistered retry policy there were no provider or infrastructure failures and no excluded seeds; the run produced a complete paired dataset and a reconciliation check confirmed accounting consistency. The archived execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle enumerate every per‑task response, validator decision, and repair trace; readers should consult those archived artifacts for per‑item inspection rather than file‑level bookkeeping in the text.

Primary outcomes (artifact‑derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts derived from the archived contingency table are n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to these counts yields p = 1.00. The observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729), as recorded in the analysis outputs. The single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]).

Post‑hoc sensitivity quantification: Because the paired estimand equals (n10 − n01)/300, any absolute paired improvement is integer‑quantized to multiples of 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction from the assumed baseline pass rate 0.40) mapped to an intended absolute change ≈ +0.30 (i.e., n10 − n01 = 90 under N=300). The observed discordant total (n10 + n01 = 1) imposes a hard resolution limit: the maximum resolvable absolute change in this run is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Consequently, the preregistered power calculation (which assumed a much higher baseline failure prevalence) is not applicable to the observed data; with only a single discordance the two‑sided exact McNemar test is inherently uninformative about large preregistered effects, producing p = 1.00. Put differently, to detect the preregistered absolute target (+0.30) at N=300 the run would have needed on the order of tens of discordant pairs (n10 substantially larger than observed); the archived contingency counts concretely demonstrate why the preregistered hypothesis could not be supported here.

Representative diagnostics: Validator traces archived for every episode include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flags. The single baseline failure was flagged by the validator, corrected by the preregistered repair prompt/adapter, and revalidated; the repair trace and final validator decision are archived. These per‑item artifacts substantiate the aggregated counts reported above.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline fully remediated the single observed baseline invalid output, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can correct validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, the experiment does not provide confirmatory evidence for the preregistered large effect (≥50% relative reduction) because the empirical baseline success rate (~99.7%) was far higher than the planning assumption (0.40), eliminating statistical headroom.

Design lessons for confirmatory NetOps evaluation: (1) Calibrate task difficulty and target initial failure prevalence during preregistration. Power calculations that assume a particular baseline pass rate can become invalid if the task bank yields a markedly different failure prevalence; we therefore recommend preregistering target initial‑failure counts (not only N) and validating the task bank prior to the run. (2) Explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets. Reusing a shared_initial_candidate reduces informative discordance and therefore reduces paired test sensitivity for a fixed N; independent draws increase discordance potential but introduce cross‑arm heterogeneity. (3) Match the repair budget to the operational claim: production guardrails often permit multiple automated repair iterations plus human approval; bounded budgets affect both realism and inferential power. (4) When operational claims require runtime assurances, incorporate emulation/simulation that exercises packet‑level or control‑plane consequences rather than relying solely on static configuration validators.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design choice and by the single allowed repair iteration. Construct validity is limited because the deterministic validator evaluates canonicalized AST and constraint satisfaction rather than executing configurations in live devices; runtime packet‑level or control‑plane effects were not measured. External validity is constrained by the synthetic task bank, limited vendor‑template space, a single model family (gpt-5-mini), and a single validator implementation. Conclusion validity is limited because only one informative discordant pair was observed; statistical inference about large preregistered effects is therefore not supported.

Recommendations for future work: Future confirmatory runs should (a) calibrate the task bank to produce a prespecified number of initial failures so that discordant‑pair counts will be informative for the paired estimand; (b) consider independent per‑arm generation semantics when larger discordance is required for inferential sensitivity; (c) increase automated repair budget or include staged human approval when testing operationally realistic remediation; (d) couple deterministic validators to emulation/execution steps when runtime effects must be guaranteed.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) evaluating a frozen deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps experiments should preregister target initial‑failure counts, explicitly state pairing semantics and repair budgets, and incorporate emulation when runtime guarantees are required. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run and enumerated in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle cited in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
